alignment.note: Greek imperfect ἐδίδασκεν ('was teaching') is rendered in Syriac periphrastically with the auxiliary ܗܘܐ (ܘܡܠܦ ܗܘܐ), the standard Syriac means of expressing durative past aspect. The Vulgate imperfect docebat matches the Greek aspect directly.

Greek coordinates two finite verbs (καὶ ἔλεγεν, 'and was saying'); the Vulgate subordinates the second verb as a present participle (dicens), while Syriac retains a coordinated finite verb (ܘܐܡܪ). The participial construction in Latin is a stylistic simplification of the Semitic-style verbal parataxis.

Greek οὐ introduces a question expecting an affirmative answer ('is it not written?'); the Vulgate captures this nuance with the interrogative particle Nonne, whereas Syriac uses the plain negative ܠܐ, leaving the interrogative force to be inferred from context and intonation.

Greek recitative ὅτι introduces the direct quotation and is matched by the Vulgate's Quia (with preceding colon). In Syriac the quotative force is absorbed into the proclitic ܕ- prefixed to ܕܒܝܬܝ, so no separate token corresponds; this is a normal feature of Syriac syntax rather than an omission of content.

Greek article+noun+pronoun (ὁ οἶκός μου) and Latin domus mea are both rendered in Syriac by the single suffixed form ܕܒܝܬܝ ('my house'), the Semitic possessive suffix economising three Greek tokens into one.

The citation of Isa 56:7 ('for all the nations') is preserved in all three; Greek πᾶσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν and Latin omnibus gentibus are matched by Syriac ܠܟܠܗܘܢ ܥܡܡܐ, with the interrogative punctuation closing the quotation in Greek and Latin.

Greek perfect πεποιήκατε with separate accusative pronoun αὐτόν and Latin fecistis eam are condensed in Syriac into the single inflected form ܥܒܕܬܘܢܝܗܝ, which incorporates both the 2nd plural subject and the 3rd masc. singular object suffix.

Greek λῃστῶν ('of robbers/bandits') is matched by Latin latronum and Syriac ܕܠܣܛܝܐ; the Syriac form is in fact a loanword from the Greek λῃστής, a common phenomenon in the Peshitta's rendering of technical or vivid Greek vocabulary.
